units.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027? Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation to the board; board meeting, January 2027
Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research
Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
Market: the market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it
US quick-commerce GMV grew 42% a year, 2022–25 (CAGR 2022–25 = (5.1 / 1.8)^(1/3) − 1 = 41.5%)
US quick-commerce grocery GMV, $ billions: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6 (+44%); 2024 3.6 (+38%); 2025 5.1 (+42%); year-on-year growth shown under each year
Both incumbents lose money on every order (EBITDA margins −26% and −46%)
Incumbent operators, 2025: Zipcart (national) revenue $1,200M, EBITDA −$310M, EBITDA margin −26%; QuickBasket (regional) revenue $210M, EBITDA −$96M, EBITDA margin −46%
Contribution per order is −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket)
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025
Zipcart footprint signal: positive in only its densest city, and only after a fee rise (p. 10)
Quick commerce is growing 42% a year, but both incumbents lose money on every order and one is already retreating

So what: the market's growth is real, but none of it has become profit. 'Nobody owns the Midwest' may simply mean nobody has made it pay. Growth does not justify entry on its own; the per-order economics have to.
Economics: a Parcelbird dark store would lose money on every order, and customers don't stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost
Loss of $6.17 per order at benchmark median (contribution after site fixed cost −$6.17)
Loss of $1.76 per order with best-observed inputs on every driver; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order
Only the founders' plan (+$2.02) is profitable, and it beats the best site ever observed on all four drivers
Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order (contribution after site cost −$12.57)
22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month 3, at 3.1 orders a month (observed behaviour)
Funding: even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints
The launch needs $9.5M; only $7.2M can be spent while keeping 12 months of runway
Adding today's core burn, cash runs out in month 13
At benchmark economics, 9 stores would lose $18M a year; a mature 9-store network loses about $18M a year ($1.5M a month), more than our total cash every year
Alternative: the software business is a better use of the same cash
The software business breaks even in about month 26 at today's 60% growth (month 36 at 40%)
Software-first never drops below 12 months of runway, provided growth stays at 34% or more; it can reach break-even within current cash if growth stays at 34% or more
Selling store-based fast delivery to pipeline grocers gives Parcelbird a share of the market's growth
We ask the board to make four decisions in January 2027 and review progress in 90 days

Decision 1: decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now and do not extend the pop-up. Do not commit capex to dark stores and do not extend the pop-up (annualised loss about $1.3M). Keep the pop-up data and cohort learning. Owner: Board; by Jan 2027

Decision 2: approve the software scale-up: 2 engineers and 2 sales hires ($0.8M a year), phased against signed contracts, released in two tranches tied to signed late-stage contracts (9 grocers, $0.86M ARR). Owner: CEO; by Q1 2027

Decision 3: build a store-based fast-delivery offer for the grocers in the pipeline: package picking and rider dispatch for grocers who want fast delivery from existing stores; test it with late-stage pipeline accounts. Owner: CTO / Sales; by Q2 2027

Decision 4: adopt explicit re-entry triggers, tracked through our customers' sites, before quick commerce is reconsidered, and runway reporting: quarterly dashboard of the 4 triggers from customer-site data, plus monthly runway against the 12-month rule. Owner: CFO; by Q1 2027
90-day checkpoint (April 2027): late-stage conversions against the 9 grocers, pilot interest in store-based fast delivery, actual ARR growth against the 34% minimum, and the first trigger dashboard
If growth is tracking below 34%, hold the second tranche of hires
We started from the founders' answer, 'launch', and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them
Initial hypothesis tested: 'Parcelbird should launch Parcelbird Now: 9 dark stores in 3 cities, contribution-positive per order by month 18.'

Condition 1 (Market): the market has a profit pool, not just growth. Evidence: GMV +42% a year, but contribution per order is −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket); QuickBasket shut 36% of its cities. Verdict: Not met
Condition 2 (Economics): a dark store makes money per order at achievable inputs. Evidence: −$6.17 per order at benchmark median; −$1.76 even with every best-observed input combined. Verdict: Not met

Condition 3 (Economics): Parcelbird runs stores better than the benchmark. Evidence: the pop-up was below the median on all four drivers (AOV, promotions, rider productivity, density). Verdict: Not shown
Condition 4 (Economics): customers stay long enough to repay acquisition cost. Evidence: $38 CAC; 22% still ordering in month 3; CAC is never repaid at benchmark or pop-up economics. Verdict: Not met
Condition 5 (Funding): the plan fits current cash with 12 months of runway. Evidence: $9.5M needed vs $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; no new funding expected. Verdict: Not met
Condition 6 (Alternative): it beats the best other use of the cash. Evidence: the software business can reach break-even within current cash if growth stays at 34% or more. Verdict: Not met
So what: the hypothesis fails on every condition, so we reverse it. The rest of the deck sets out the evidence in the order of the table.
At benchmark-median inputs a Parcelbird store would lose $6.17 per order; $2.67 of that is lost before any site cost, so more volume cannot fix it

Contribution per order at benchmark median (14 customer sites, 2025), $: goods margin (27% × $34) +9.18; delivery fee +1.99; promotions (6% × $34) −2.04; picking & packing −3.10; rider ($17.75 ÷ 2.4) −7.40; payment & packaging −1.30; before site fixed cost −2.67; site fixed cost ($1.15M ÷ 328.5k) −3.50; after site fixed cost −6.17
Each order brings in $11.17 (goods margin plus delivery fee) and costs $13.84 in promotions, picking, riders and payment before the store's rent and staff are counted
Why volume can't fix it: higher density spreads the $3.50 of site cost over more orders, but each extra order still loses $2.67
The model only turns positive if AOV or rider productivity rise sharply
Biggest cost line: riders, $7.40 per order, 81% of the goods margin
Two of our three cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers
Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order
Contribution per order before site fixed cost by scenario: Columbus pop-up (actual) −$6.21; benchmark median −$2.67; best observed (all drivers) +$0.49; founders' plan +$3.77
Contribution per order after site fixed cost by scenario: Columbus pop-up (actual) −$12.57; benchmark median −$6.17; best observed (all drivers) −$1.76; founders' plan +$2.02
No site has achieved the best-observed case: the best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 orders/day) come from different sites. Combining them is already optimistic, and it still loses money.
Nine stores at network scale: median −$18.2M a year; best observed −$8.1M a year; founders' plan +$11.9M a year. Only the plan's inputs give a profitable network.
Break-even AOV: with other inputs held, the median store needs an AOV of $63 and the best-observed store $50. The median is $34 and the best ever observed is $42.
Break-even AOV (other inputs held; solve contribution after site cost = 0): pop-up $115; median $63; best obs. $50; plan $37

Definition: 'Before site fixed cost' covers the variable costs of each order. 'After' also spreads each store's $1.15M a year of rent, staff and utilities (pop-up: $0.65M) across its orders. Both figures exclude HQ overhead, capex and marketing.
Pop-up scenario inputs: AOV / promotions $31 / 12%; orders per rider-hour 2.1; orders per site per day 280
Benchmark median scenario inputs: AOV / promotions $34 / 6%; orders per rider-hour 2.4; orders per site per day 900
Best observed scenario inputs: AOV / promotions $42 / 6%; orders per rider-hour 3.0; orders per site per day 1,400
Founders' plan scenario inputs: AOV / promotions $45 / 2%; orders per rider-hour 3.5; orders per site per day 1,800
Profit per store per year: pop-up −$1.3M; median −$2.0M; best obs. −$0.9M; plan +$1.3M
The founders' plan needs results beyond the best site ever observed on all four drivers; if AOV or rider productivity only reaches the median, the plan loses money again
Average order value: observed range n/a; median $34; best $42; plan $45; plan vs best +7%
Promotions, % of AOV: observed pop-up 12%; median 6%; best 6%; plan 2%; plan vs best −4 pts
Orders per rider-hour: observed range 1.9–3.0; median 2.4; best 3.0; plan 3.5; plan vs best +17% above range
Orders per site per day: observed range 400–1,400; median 900; best 1,400; plan 1,800; plan vs best +29% above range
Plan profit per order if one driver is at the median: plan as proposed 2.02; AOV $45 → $34: −0.73
Plan profit per order if one driver is at the median: Riders 3.5 → 2.4 /hr: 0.22
units.correct_version: Riders 3.5 → 2.4 /hr: −$0.31 (−0.306214). The chart value is attached to the wrong driver; with rider productivity at the median the plan loses money, as the slide's title and text state.

units.text: Plan profit per order if one driver is at the median: Orders/day 1,800 → 900: −0.31
units.correct_version: Orders/day 1,800 → 900: +$0.27 (0.26781). The chart value is attached to the wrong driver; with density at the median the plan keeps a thin positive margin, as the slide's text states.

units.text: Plan profit per order if one driver is at the median: Promotions 2% → 6%: 0.27
units.correct_version: Promotions 2% → 6%: +$0.22 (0.218191). The chart value is attached to the wrong driver.

units.text: Sanity check on scale: 9 stores × 1,800 orders × $45 × 365 days = $266M a year of sales in three mid-size cities. That is more than QuickBasket's total 2025 revenue ($210M) across all its cities, and about 5% of the entire 2025 US market ($5.1B).
This compares our GMV with their reported revenue, which we take to be roughly equivalent for an operator that sells the goods itself
The plan is most exposed to AOV and rider productivity, the two drivers it stretches furthest
Falling short on density or promotions alone still leaves a thin positive margin of about $0.2–0.3 per order, but nothing for HQ overhead or marketing
Our own Columbus pop-up came in below the benchmark median on every driver, so there is no evidence yet that we run stores better than others
Pop-up (6 weeks) vs median: average order value $31 vs $34 (−9%); promotions 12% vs 6% (2× higher); orders per rider-hour 2.1 vs 2.4 (−13%); orders per site per day 280 vs 900 (−69%)

The founders' case for a capability edge: 'Our software already runs other people's dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone.' The pop-up is the only test of this, and it did worse than the median of the stores our software runs.

Fair caveat: it was early. Six weeks on a temporary site. Orders grew 18% a week, from roughly 179 a day in week 1 to roughly 408 in week 6 (our estimate from the compounding). But that growth came with 12% promotions and $38 of acquisition cost per customer.
Implication: even if density reached the median, the store would still lose $6.17 per order (p. 5). Ramp-up alone does not close the gap.
Pop-up site cost: $650,000 a year ÷ (280 × 365 orders) = $6.36 per order. Rider cost: $17.75 ÷ 2.1 = $8.45 per order.
Customers don't stay long enough to repay their $38 acquisition cost: 44% say they would order weekly, but only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month 3
44% of 1,500 surveyed Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery 'at least weekly' (stated intent, one age group only)
0.68 orders a month per acquired customer by month 3 (22% × 3.1)
Months to repay $38 of acquisition cost: Columbus pop-up (−$6.21 per order before site cost): never; benchmark median (−$2.67): never
Months to repay $38 of acquisition cost: best observed (+$0.49 per order before site cost): 77 orders to repay, 113 months (~9 years)
Months to repay $38 of acquisition cost: founders' plan (+$3.77 per order before site cost): 10 orders to repay, 15 months
Months = ($38 ÷ contribution per order) ÷ 0.68 orders per acquired customer per month. This is generous: it assumes no churn after month 3 and uses contribution before any site cost.

So what: buying growth with promotions and paid social does not create value at these economics. At the median, every customer acquired adds to the losses. Even under the founders' plan, payback takes more than a year.
Zipcart's one profitable city needed a $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions, and it lost 14% of its volume; the same moves on our median store still lose $1.05 per order

Applying Zipcart's Q4 2025 moves to the benchmark-median store, contribution after site cost, $/order: benchmark median −6.17; +$3.99 service fee (+3.99); promotions 6% → 1% (+1.70); volume −14%: site cost per order (−0.57); with Zipcart moves −1.05

What the investor update leaves out: 'Zipcart turned contribution-positive (+$0.40 per order)' was true only for its densest city, after a new $3.99 fee on every order and a cut in promotions to 1%. Volume in that city then fell 14%.

What it would take for us: with those moves, a median store before site cost earns +$3.02 per order. To cover $1.15M of site cost it needs about 1,042 orders a day after the fee rise: 16% above today's median, 3.7× the pop-up, and with no loss of rider productivity at the lower volume.
Read-across: a profitable route may exist, but only at top-quartile density with premium pricing. This is not where a new entrant starts, and nothing in our data shows it yet.
Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the 12-month runway rule, and with today's core burn added it runs out of cash by month 13
Cash available for Parcelbird Now vs. founders' requirement, $M: cash in bank 12; 12-month runway floor (12 × $0.4M) 4.8; spendable 7.2; founders' cash need to month 18 9.5; shortfall 2.3

If the $9.5M is in addition to today's $0.4M a month of core burn: with software ARR still growing 60% a year, cash falls below 12 months of runway in month 5 and below zero in month 13 (model, p. 14)
Even if the $9.5M covered all company spending: $12.0M − $9.5M = $2.5M left at month 18: about 6 months of runway at today's burn, against the 12 required
The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator 'unlikely'
The floor rises once stores are operating, because a higher burn needs a larger reserve to cover 12 months. The $7.2M of headroom is therefore a ceiling.
Of the three options, only software-first meets both investor constraints and keeps a foothold in fast delivery (C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers: recommended)
Three options compared: A. Launch Parcelbird Now (9 dark stores, 3 cities); B. One permanent pilot store (Columbus); C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers (recommended)
Option A, per-order economics: No: −$6.17 median; positive only on plan inputs
Option A, cash need: No: $9.5M to month 18 (plan)
Option A, 12-month runway rule: No: breached in month 5; cash out in month 13
Option A, path to profit within current cash: No: only if every driver beats the best observed
Option A, strategic fit: No: competes with the grocers we sell to; distracts the team
Option A, main risk: unit economics never close; cash runs out
Option B, per-order economics: No: −$6.17 median; −$12.57 pop-up actual
Option B, cash need: Partly: $0.6M capex + ~$2.0M a year loss
Option B, 12-month runway rule: No: breached in month 10
Option B, path to profit within current cash: No: none: a single store cannot reach scale
Option B, strategic fit: Partly: little new learning: pop-up and 14-site data already exist
Option B, main risk: losses with no route to scale
Option C, per-order economics: Yes: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts
Option C, cash need: Yes: $0.8M a year of hires, phased
Option C, 12-month runway rule: Yes: never below 24 months at 60% growth
Option C, path to profit within current cash: Yes: break-even in month 26 (60%) or 36 (40%)
Option C, strategic fit: Yes: meets demand already in the pipeline
Option C, main risk: ARR growth falls below 34% a year
Runway and break-even figures come from the monthly cash model (p. 13–14) and assume software ARR grows 60% a year unless stated
Cash under each option: A runs out in month 13, B drifts to near zero, and C bottoms out at $5.4M before the business turns cash-positive
Runway < 12 months: A. Launch month 5; B. Pilot month 10; C. Software-first never. Lowest cash: A −$2.5M; B $0.2M; C $5.4M
Model assumptions: software ARR +60% a year in all three options. Today's burn ($0.4M a month) = software opex − gross profit. Opex is held flat apart from the $0.8M hires (in B and C, not in A).
A: $5.4M capex at one store a month (months 1–9), plus the plan's other $4.1M spread evenly over months 1–18 and nothing after. This is the founders' best case.
B: $0.6M capex, then the median store's −$2.0M a year
Runway = cash ÷ recurring monthly burn
Software-first stays within current cash and the runway rule as long as ARR keeps growing at least 34% a year, just over half today's 60%
ARR growth 60% (today's rate): break-even month 26; lowest cash $5.4M; min. runway 24 mo.
ARR growth 40%: break-even month 36; lowest cash $2.7M; min. runway 18 mo.
ARR growth 34% (minimum that keeps 12-month runway): break-even month 41; lowest cash $1.2M; min. runway 12 mo.
ARR growth 25%: break-even not by month 48; cash runs out; runway rule breached
Break-even ARR = opex ÷ 81% = $8.9M ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M, against $4.1M today
The pipeline supports the hires: the 9 late-stage grocers are worth $0.86M of ARR; all 37 are worth $3.55M. The $0.8M of hires pays for itself with 10 contracts (28% of the pipeline).
What has to be true: 34% growth means about 15 net new contracts in year 1, and 60% means about 26. Costs must also stay flat apart from the hires.
The pack does not give churn or win rates, so phase the hires against signed contracts
The recommendation survives the main uncertainties: most of them would make a launch worse, and the risks to software-first can be managed

Rider minimum-pay rules (2 of 3 cities): +20% rider cost = +$1.48/order at median, +$1.01 on the plan. Effect: strengthens 'don't launch'. Mitigation: none needed for C; track the rules for any future re-entry
Density in mid-size Midwest cities: pop-up 280/day vs median 900; range 400–1,400. Effect: strengthens 'don't launch'. Monitoring: Trigger 1 (p. 16) tracks density across customer sites
Raising AOV could erode the convenience use case: the plan needs $45 vs $42 best and $31 pop-up. Effect: strengthens 'don't launch'. Monitoring: Trigger 2 (p. 16)

A competitor claims the Midwest first: incumbents are retreating (QuickBasket −4 cities) and lose money per order. Effect: low: first-mover status has not created profit. Mitigation: re-entry later can use our software data

Software growth slows below the minimum: below 34% a year, C breaches the runway rule; 25% runs out of cash. Effect: main risk to C. Mitigation: phase hires against signed contracts; review cost base quarterly

Software cost base grows faster than assumed: the model holds opex flat apart from the $0.8M of hires. Effect: delays C's break-even. Mitigation: board-approved opex envelope; monthly runway reporting
Grocers' own fast delivery competes with our customers: several pipeline grocers want store-based fast delivery. Effect: upside for C. Response: package store-based fast delivery as a product

What would change our mind: reconsider an operator model only when our customers' sites show that the economics work and the funding exists. Proposed re-entry triggers, reviewed quarterly from the data our software already collects across the 14 customer sites (no extra cost)
Trigger 1, site-level profit is proven: at least one customer site shows positive contribution after site cost for two consecutive quarters. Today: none. Best-observed inputs give −$1.76.

Trigger 2, the profit drivers are seen at one site at the same time: AOV ≥ $42 and ≥ 3.0 orders per rider-hour at ≥ 1,050 orders a day, or a service fee that does the same job without losing more than 15% of volume. Today: no site has both. Break-even with Zipcart's moves needs about 1,042 orders a day.

Trigger 3, customers stay: month-3 retention high enough to repay $38 of acquisition cost within 12 months at actual contribution. Today: 22% at 3.1 orders a month, so payback never happens at the median.
Trigger 4, funding is ring-fenced: dedicated capital that leaves the core business with 12 months of runway at all times. Today: a new round is 'unlikely'; headroom is $7.2M against a $9.5M plan.

Appendix A1, pop-up per order: goods margin (27% of AOV) +$8.37; delivery fee (net) +$1.99; promotions −$3.72; picking & packing −$3.10; rider cost −$8.45; payment & packaging −$1.30; contribution before site fixed cost −$6.21; site fixed cost per order −$6.36; contribution after site fixed cost −$12.57; per store per year −$1.3M

Appendix A1, best observed per order: goods margin +$11.34; delivery fee (net) +$1.99; promotions −$2.52; picking & packing −$3.10; rider cost −$5.92; payment & packaging −$1.30; contribution before site fixed cost +$0.49; site fixed cost per order −$2.25; contribution after site fixed cost −$1.76; per store per year −$0.9M

Appendix A1, founders' plan per order: goods margin +$12.15; delivery fee (net) +$1.99; promotions −$0.90; picking & packing −$3.10; rider cost −$5.07; payment & packaging −$1.30; contribution before site fixed cost +$3.77; site fixed cost per order −$1.75; contribution after site fixed cost +$2.02; per store per year +$1.3M

Appendix A1 calculations: goods margin = AOV × 27%; delivery fee $1.99, net of payment cost; promotions = AOV × promo %; picking & packing $3.10 per order; rider cost = $17.75 ÷ orders per rider-hour; payment & packaging $1.30 per order; site fixed cost per order = annual fixed ÷ (orders/day × 365); per store per year = × orders/day × 365

Inputs: Table 3 and section 7 of the briefing pack. Pop-up site fixed cost is $650k a year; all others are $1.15M. Promotions are treated as a cost on AOV and goods margin as 27% of AOV before promotions. HQ overhead, capex and marketing are excluded.
Judgement call, 'contribution per order': the founders and incumbents don't define it; we show it both before and after site fixed cost. Does it change the answer? No: the median is negative on both

Judgement call, founders' $9.5M: unclear whether it includes the core $0.4M a month of burn; we show both readings: on top of core burn (cash out in month 13) and all-in ($2.5M left at month 18). Does it change the answer? No: both breach the 12-month rule
Judgement call, runway definition ('12 months of runway at all times'): cash ÷ recurring monthly burn; one-off capex excluded from the burn (lenient). Does it change the answer? No
Judgement call, software cost base: the pack gives burn, not opex; opex = 81% × ARR + burn; held flat apart from the $0.8M hires. Optimistic for C; hence the 34% minimum and phased hires
Judgement call, pilot option (B): not in the pack; one permanent store at median economics, $0.6M capex. Does it change the answer? No
Judgement call, GMV vs revenue: operators' revenue is roughly their GMV; used only for the scale sanity check (p. 7). Does it change the answer? No
Judgement call, pop-up ramp: only the average and weekly growth are given; assumed constant 18% weekly compounding over 6 weeks. Does it change the answer? No
